faq.q: Why is the femoral triangle important in low‑resource settings?

exam: What bedside test would you perform to confirm a suspected femoral nerve injury and why? — Test: Knee extension strength; weakness indicates femoral nerve involvement.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden thigh pain and swelling. Which anatomical compartment is most at risk and what is your immediate management? — Anterior compartment; give analgesia, hydrate, and arrange urgent imaging.

How does malaria‑induced splenomegaly alter the relationship of the splenic artery to surrounding structures? — The enlarged spleen displaces the artery medially, increasing risk of rupture during palpation.

During a trauma exam you find a palpable step‑off at the mid‑shaft of the femur. Which spot‑question concept helps you decide the next step? — Identify the location, assess neuro‑vascular status, then immobilise and arrange radiography.

Explain why a distal tibial fracture may compromise the posterior tibial artery in a patient with peripheral arterial disease. — The fracture can lacerate the artery; compromised flow worsens ischaemia in already diseased limbs.

What are the key differences on ultrasound between a simple muscle strain and a compartmental haematoma? — Strain shows focal fibre disruption; haematoma appears as an anechoic fluid collection with possible clot.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has a swollen knee with limited flexion. Which anatomical structure should you examine first and why? — The popliteal fossa; swelling may compress the popliteal artery and vein, threatening limb viability.
Why is it unsafe to perform a blind femoral nerve block in a patient with severe coagulopathy? — The needle may injure the femoral artery or vein, causing uncontrolled bleeding.

ai.summary: A concise guide to using anatomy spot questions for rapid recall of key structures, relations and clinical relevance in low‑resource settings. Focuses on bedside thinking rather than rote memorisation.

Link each structure to a common clinical scenario (e.g., femoral nerve block, malaria‑related splenomegaly).
sections.p: Anatomy spot questions present a single structure or region and ask you to identify its location, relations and clinical importance. They train you to visualise anatomy in the patient’s body, which is essential for ward‑round examinations and procedural safety.

sections.p: Describe what lies anterior, posterior, medial and lateral to the structure, and any important fascial planes.

In tropical settings, consider embolic malaria or sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion.
sections.p: State the arterial source, venous drainage and any anastomoses that may preserve tissue viability when a main vessel is compromised.
